Function map

Source: vignettes/articles/function-map.Rmd
function-map.Rmd

This page maps the functions of mortensor onto the steps of an analysis and shows how their results feed into each other. Each box names a function and its main purpose. Paths through the maps are workflows; the section “What is not covered” lists steps that need other tools.

The main path

Every analysis passes the same objects from top to bottom. The boxes are objects; the labels on the arrows are the functions that connect them.

Map 1: from tables to analysis-ready data

The steps in their usual order. Each is a decision about the data; skip those a data set does not need. Every step returns an mt_data object.

Smoothing is not a step of this map. mt_smooth() with mt_smooth_check() and mt_plot_smooth() shows what a smoother would do to the data; for forecasts, smooth inside the fit with step_smooth() (map 2), so that observation noise and backtests refer to the raw deaths. mt_fit() warns about data smoothed beforehand and mt_backtest() refuses them.

Map 2: models, coherence and evaluation

A model specification is one model, optionally inside wrappers. Preprocessing steps given as prep are repeated in every fit, so that backtests do not see the test years.

Choosing between specifications:

tuned() and mt_tune() run the same comparison inside a fit, over a grid of model and preprocessing settings (for example the number of components and the smoothing of hyndman_ullah(), or the fitting window), with rolling origins or a single hold-out of the last years. recalibrated() keeps the chosen model and rescales the width of its intervals.

Map 3: from draws to results

Indicators and comparisons are computed path by path, so their intervals include the joint uncertainty of all strata. The same functions describe observed data.

What is not covered

These steps of a mortality analysis need other tools or are open development points:

  • Population projections. mortensor forecasts death rates; future exposures (for expected deaths) come from a population projection, for example of the statistical office, passed as exposure.
  • Spatial models for small areas. There is no model with spatial smoothing between neighbouring regions (such as BYM models), and no relational model for small populations (such as TOPALS); pooling works through common trends (li_lee()); Bayesian APC models smooth over age, period and cohort within each stratum.
  • Models of life expectancy. Models that forecast life expectancy itself (such as the Bayesian models of the UN or the double-gap model) are not implemented; mortensor forecasts rates and derives life expectancy from them.
  • Multiple imputation of suppressed cells. mt_fill_suppressed() returns one estimate; the uncertainty of suppressed counts is not carried into forecasts.
  • Causes of death with changing coding. ICD revisions and coding changes (for example of dementia) are not bridged; cause groups that span the affected codes reduce the problem.
